newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S.-Kuwait $1.2 bln loan to be signed on Sept 15.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-Kuwait $1.2 bln loan to be signed on Sept 15.

text.p: A group of international and Gulf banks and financial institutions will sign an agreement this month to provide $1.2 billion in finance for a U.S.-Kuwait petrochemical complex, Gulf Investment Corp (GIC) said.

"Arrangers and underwriters of the $1.2 billion project finance transaction for Equate will be signing the loan agreement on September 15," said an official from Kuwait-based GIC, one of the arrangers.
Bankers in the Gulf say the loan is the largest non-recourse project financing ever arranged in the region outside of the crude and refining sector.
It is also the first major loan in the region to incorporate a mix of conventional and Islamic financing.
In January, the U.S.-Kuwaiti joint venture awarded a group of 14 Gulf and American banks a mandate to raise $1.2 billion in long-term financing to build the complex south of Kuwait City.

The venture between America's Union Carbide Corp, Kuwait's Petrochemical Industries Co (PIC) and Kuwait's Bubiyan Petrochemical Co turned down an offer by the U.S. Eximbank that would have covered almost all the financing.
Total cost will be about $2 billion. The non-debt portion will be obtained from the partners' equity participation.
The loan was negotiated by National Bank of Kuwait (NBK), Kuwait's largest commercial bank. NBK and 13 banks and institutions including an Islamic institution underwrote it.
Thirteen financial institutions and banks took $76.92 million each of the financing. The Islamic institution, Kuwait Finance House, will underwrite $200 million.

The 13 are Chase Manhattan, J.P. Morgan & Co, Citibank, Bahrain-based Gulf International Bank, GIC, Saudi-based Arab Petroleum Investment Corp and Arab Investment Co, Arab Banking Corp, NBK, Kuwaiti commercial banks Gulf Bank, Commercial Bank, al-Ahli Bank and Burgan Bank.
There are two tranches -- $500 million over 10-1/2 years by Kuwaiti-based institutions and $700 million for 8-1/2 years by regional and international institutions, sources said.
